t.6.52.1: Having heard those words spoken by Kumbhakarṇa, the huge-bodied, mighty one, splendid in his arms, Mahodara spoke.
t.6.52.2: Born in the family of Kumbhakarṇa, bold, of common vision and puffed up with pride, you are unable to discern what ought to be done in every situation.
t.6.52.3: For it is not that the king does not know good policy from bad, O Kumbhakarṇa; but you, excited out of boyishness, merely wish to talk.
t.6.52.5: What can only be done by a powerful man of common understanding, one who has never sat at the feet of the elders, what wise man would do such a thing?
t.6.52.4: O bull among rākṣasas, one who knows the proper division of place and time perceives the standing, the growth and the decline both of himself and of others.
t.6.52.6: As for dharma, artha and kāma, which you declare to rest on separate foundations, you truly have no natural aptitude to comprehend them.
t.6.52.8: Dharma and artha indeed bear the highest good as their fruit; with the other two, one attains adharma and anartha, and their fruit brings only ruin.
t.6.52.7: Action indeed is the very purpose of all means; and in this world deeds bear their fruit, good for some and evil for wicked deeds.
t.6.52.9: Men pursue action that bears on this world and on the world beyond; but only one who resorts to fitting actions attains what he desires.
t.6.52.10: In this matter, this course of action has been resolved upon by the king in his heart, and it is approved by us as well. For whatever bold deed may be done against an enemy, what is lost thereby?
t.6.52.11: As for the reason you have put forward for the advance of one alone, I shall tell you what is untenable in it and what is improper as well.
t.6.52.12: How will you, alone, conquer that Rāghava by whom many exceedingly mighty rākṣasas were slain before in Janasthāna?
t.6.52.13: Those mighty rākṣasas who were once vanquished by him in Janasthāna, all of them you see even today in the city, still stricken with fear.
t.6.52.14: Out of folly you wish to rouse Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, who is like an enraged lion, as one would awaken a sleeping serpent.
t.6.52.15: Who is able to approach him, ever blazing with splendour and unassailable in his wrath, unbearable like Death itself?
t.6.52.16: All this hangs in doubt when one confronts the enemy; your going there alone does not please me.
t.6.52.17: Who, with his own resources depleted, would, like a common man, seek to bring under his control an enemy whose resources are abundant, when he is surely bent on throwing away his life?
t.6.52.19: Having thus spoken to the enraged Kumbhakarṇa, Mahodara then addressed Rāvaṇa, who makes the worlds cry out, in the midst of the rākṣasas.
t.6.52.18: O best of rākṣasas, how can you hope to fight one who has no equal among men, one who is the equal of Indra and Vivasvat?
t.6.52.20: Having obtained that Vaidehī once more, why do you prattle on? Whenever you wish, Sītā will then come under your control.
t.6.52.22: "I, Dvijihva, Saṃhrādī, Kumbhakarṇa and Vitardana: these five are setting out for the slaying of Rāma. Proclaim this aloud!"
t.6.52.21: I have found a certain means that would bring Sītā to wait upon you; if it pleases your own judgment, O lord of the rākṣasas, hear it.
t.6.52.23: Then, going forth, we shall give him battle with all our effort; if we conquer your enemies, we have no need of stratagems.
t.6.52.24: But if our enemy still lives even after we have fought the battle, then we shall resort to what we have resolved in our minds.
t.6.52.25: We shall come back here from the battle drenched in blood, our own bodies torn open by sharp arrows marked with the name of Rāma.
t.6.52.27: Then, O king, have it proclaimed throughout the city from the back of an elephant, on every side: "Rāma has been slain together with his brother and his army!"
t.6.52.26: Declaring, “Rāghava has been devoured by us, and Lakṣmaṇa too,” we shall clasp your feet; now fulfill our desire.
t.6.52.28: Then, O subduer of enemies, being truly pleased, have enjoyments, retinues, the objects of their desires and wealth bestowed upon your servants.
t.6.52.30: Then, when this rumour has grown strong and spread everywhere, you should enter, reassure Sītā and console her in private; and tempt her with wealth and grain, with objects of desire and with jewels.
t.6.52.31: By this stratagem, O king, attended by fear and grief, Sītā, her protector lost, will come under your control even against her will.
t.6.52.29: Then take the garlands, garments and unguent of the heroes, and plenty of drink from the warriors, and you yourself, delighted, drink!
t.6.52.32: For when she learns that her husband, the one who delights her heart, has perished, she, out of despair and the fickleness of a woman's nature, will submit to your will.
t.6.52.33: She who was formerly raised in comfort, who is worthy of comfort and is now worn down by sorrow, will, knowing that happiness depends upon you, come to you in every way.
t.6.52.34: This is sound policy in my view, for merely by seeing Rāma misfortune would arise. Your purpose will be accomplished right here; do not be impatient. Great is the gain of happiness won without battle.
t.6.52.35: Indeed, O lord of men, one who conquers his enemies without battle, his army undestroyed and himself never falling into peril, enjoys for a long time great fame and merit, O king, as well as prosperity and renown.
